newsitem.title: ITALY: Lawyer says ex-SS Priebke's mental health worrying.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says ex-SS Priebke's mental health worrying.

text.p: A lawyer for former SS captain Erich Priebke, who is being held in a military prison, said on Monday the German's mental health was declining and his long confinement was in violation of human rights.
"(Priebke) has been in a state of intellectual bewilderment for several days," defence lawyer Carlo Taormina told Reuters.

He said that Priebke was increasingly withdrawn and that doctors were worried that given his age -- 83 -- he could lose some of his brain functions. Asked if that meant senility, Taormina said "this is something that is inevitably linked".

A court ruled last month that Priebke, detained in Rome since his extradition from Argentina in November 1995, must stay in a Rome military prison while he awaits retrial for participation in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity.
The case is now in limbo because both military and civilian courts have said they do not have the jurisdiction to try him.
Priebke's first trial ended in uproar last year after judges ruled that he could go free, but he was rearrested immediately and the original ruling was later thrown out on appeal.
Taormina said he planned to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg because he alleged that Italy's continued detention of Priebke "trampled on" fundamental human rights.

Italy sought Priebke's extradition after he admitted to a U.S. television crew in the Andean resort of Bariloche, his home for nearly 50 years, that he took part in the SS massacre of 335 men and boys in the Ardeatine Caves near Rome on March 24, 1944.
The Court of Cassation, Italy's highest court, is due to decide on February 10 whether the retrial should take place in a military or civilian court.
Priebke has admitted he shot two people at the Ardeatine Caves and crossed off names from a list as victims were led inside. He argues he had to follow orders or be killed himself.
The massacre was ordered in retaliation for a partisan bomb attack in Rome the day before which killed 33 members of the German occupying forces.
